title: We’re All Jane Doe: How To Center Survivors When Talking About The Cornell 7 Rape Case
text:
We’re All Jane Doe: How To Center Survivors When Talking About The Cornell 7 Rape Case

Content warning: This article contains descriptions of or allusions to rape and sexual abuse. 

This is an op-ed by Farrah Khan, a consent educator, gender justice advocate for sexual assault survivors and survivor herself.

By now, you’ve probably seen the headlines. It’s the most talked-about court case in the world: About a week after a fraternity party at Cornell in October 2024, Jane Doe was scrolling an anonymous online forum about Greek life when she came across a post about a sophomore who had been allegedly gang-raped at the Chi Phi house. She was that sophomore. Until then, she had only heard rumors going around campus that she was a slut. She later told investigators, after filing a complaint last month in a New York court, that reading that post was the first time her experience was validated and “the narrative change[d] that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted.” Those words come from records of Cornell’s Title IX investigation, reported by The New York Times, following the diligent reporting by student journalists Cereese Qusba and Sophia Dasser, who broke the story. Jane Doe went on to report the assault and sue the university. Prosecutors have reopened the case and say they will take it to a grand jury. Lawyers for at least three of the men deny any wrongdoing. The case has sparked a global discussion on sexual assault, campus safety, fraternity culture, and the frustrations survivors feel in the face of institutions that fail them.

Stories like Jane Doe’s will keep emerging. What the conversation has been missing is how we respond when, like her, someone in our lives discloses their assault, and to every survivor who sees themselves in her story.

When I read about Jane Doe and the Cornell 7, a painful buzz began pulsing in my chest. My hands grew clammy. My breath got caught in my throat. I know intimately how easy it is to internalize shame. I felt the same shame when it happened to me.

In my first year of university, a group of us went to a friend’s cottage. It was me, a close girlfriend, her boyfriend, and the guy whose cottage it was, someone I’d known for years. I thought I could trust him. We all drank Blue Curaçao the first night and then crashed in our separate bedrooms. In the middle of the night, I woke up with him on top of me. I asked, “What are we doing?” as if I had some control over what he had chosen to do to me.

When I pushed him off, he slurred, “You’re always open. Slut.” I froze on the bed while he twisted the sheets around his body and passed out. The dread of self-blame kept me in that bed all night. I believed him. It was easier than facing the fact that someone I was friends with would do that.

The next morning, I pulled my girlfriend into the bathroom and told her what had happened. The first thing she said was, “You’re not going to tell anybody, are you? It’s going to ruin the trip.” I got really small then and spent the weekend doing what everyone else was: I pretended it never happened. I kept thinking, maybe it was me. It wasn’t a big deal. I shouldn’t have talked about it like that. I shouldn’t have had a drink. I shouldn’t have worn a tank top and shorts.

The smell of Blue Curaçao will forever make me gag.

This wasn’t my first time being subjected to sexual assault; like most women I know, it isn’t just one thing. It’s the joke in sixth grade about your body, a family member sitting too close, the guys who yelled vulgar words from their car, the boyfriend or girlfriend who doesn’t stop. It’s cumulative; it wears us all down to know we live in a society that doesn’t prioritize safety, let alone protect us.

Now, I’ve spent more than 20 years on the other side of those conversations. I started as a teenager, writing a zine about how to support a friend who tells you they’ve been harmed. I became a counselor. I ran a sexual assault support center at a university, where I sat with students in the early morning hours after frat parties. I led a national project on gender-based violence on campuses, and was part of the first Gender Equality advisory for the G7, where I was the first survivor to ever address G7 leaders, including the current president. “I speak as a survivor,” I started my address. “I speak as a survivor, and I speak with the survivors who cannot be in this room. And I carry with them the hope that nobody else has to say ‘Me Too.’”

Most students who are sexually assaulted never go to campus resources or to the police, according to the AAU’s 2019 national campus survey. They tell their people — friends, family, co-workers. In reports from schools that shared their results, about four in five women who were assaulted told someone, usually a friend. This isn’t the stranger in the white van, this is someone they know which makes reporting so much harder.

So the first response a survivor gets usually comes from a friend, not a counselor or an investigator. The Cornell survivor’s account of her alleged assault was first affirmed not by the administration at her school but by a stranger online, then by a roommate brave enough to say it.

When I think about that cottage weekend, it isn’t his words; it’s my friend’s that stick in my ribs. How we respond to someone who tells us they have been sexually assaulted is world-building. Every time we respond to a sexual assault disclosure with care, we practice leaving behind a world that tells men they have impunity and women to comply, because there is no place to be safe. Part of my own world-building was reading Audre Lorde, Maya Angelou, and Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha. Their words taught me that the burden of sexual violence wasn’t mine to carry. Inspired by them, I created a cut-and-paste zine for survivors called SOAR, with five simple steps to support survivors. Decades later, it became the BRAVE model, which I use in my professional training. It’s broken down into five steps: Begin by Listening (start by listening, and let them know you believe them), Respect (respect their privacy and their choices), Ask (ask what support looks like to them, instead of assuming, Validate (let them know that their feelings make sense and that it wasn’t their fault) and Empathize (your presence matters more than perfect words). More than 100,000 people have since been trained in this model, on campuses and in youth programs, nonprofits, healthcare settings, and government agencies. It started as a peer tool, and it uses plain language on purpose because you don’t need to be an expert to support someone.

Since the Cornell story broke, women and gender diverse people have been posting “I am Jane Doe” and sharing stories — some from last month and some from decades ago. They are doing so to make sure Cornell’s Jane Doe doesn’t get doxxed, and also to be in community with other survivors. But alongside those stories is a flood of victim-blaming. It’s important to remember that survivors in your life are reading these posts.

It’s not just online. Disclosures of sexual assault by survivors are being shared between friends over drinks, with a crush or with a co-worker before a team retreat. That’s part of what happens when a major story of sexual assault breaks: people grieve, remember, and share. This happened when the Hockey Canada story broke, too. And it’s going to keep happening.

Here’s how BRAVE can help you support a survivor.

DashDividers_1_500x100

What do you do if someone tells you they were assaulted? Begin by listening

When the group chat is buzzing, a message might come in privately: “This whole thing is bringing up a lot for me.” If we are not feeling grounded, a panicked response sounds like: “Wait, what happened?? Who was it? Did you report it?” Every question comes from love, but together they put the survivor on the spot. BRAVE is a practice that starts with a breath and a pause.

Listening means noticing who isn’t talking. A screenshot of the Cornell story lands in a group chat. And someone goes quiet. Check in. More than half of women in the U.S. have been subjected to sexual violence involving physical contact, and for more than 80% of women who’ve been raped, this happened to them before they turned 25. On campus, it’s about one in four undergraduate women. Sexual assault should not be the price women have to pay to graduate.

Look at your chat. Count. Even if you’re not a survivor yourself, chances are there is someone in your chat affected by sexual assault. They may be afraid to say anything, not knowing if they can trust anyone with what they are going through.

Sexual harassment or assault doesn’t start in college either. This summer, I led a workshop with a group of high school girls in a small suburb. We collaged together what a future grown with consent would feel like. While gluing torn paper and glitter stars together, we discussed barriers to reporting. One participant said, “It’s too late. Why would I tell anyone? No one believed me when I was a kid.” Then, one by one, every girl in the room said something similar. I wanted to breathe fire. Instead, I found a way to ground myself. Take a breath, squish my toes into the ground and breathe. “This is a lot,” I said. “I’m glad you’re here.”

Disclosure is rarely linear. Survivors can tell it sideways at first, as a joke, or recounting a “crazy night” similar to what Jane Doe shared with her roommate. Her roommate’s instincts to listen and reflect on what she heard are part of interrupting harm.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Their assault isn’t grounds for gossip. Respect confidentiality

When my friend at the cottage asked me not to tell anybody, she was asking me to protect her needs. Confidentiality is supposed to protect the survivor’s choice, not everyone else’s comfort.

Survivors get to choose if, when and how they want to share their story. Most college students who are sexually assaulted never report it to their school or the police, according to the AAU. That decision belongs to them. It’s rarely simple. When researchers read through nearly 1,300 #WhyIDidntReport posts from college survivors, the reasons sounded so familiar to me: the blame they’d already turned on themselves, who the person who hurt them was, and how the decision only got harder with time.

When someone tells you, you might feel the urge to tell someone else. But only the survivor decides if, when, and how they want to talk about it.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Let the survivor lead. Ask what support looks like

Support isn’t one-size-fits-all. For some people, it’s seeing a counsellor. Support can look like going to the hospital with a friend to get a forensic kit. It could be a night on the couch watching a TV show or movie with friends. For others, it’s time, because maybe they’re not ready to talk yet. So ask: “What do you need right now? How can I be here for you?” Then let them choose. In one 2025 study, survivors described what they wished people had said, and the researchers took their title from one of them: “I want more personalized support.” And when survivors share online, one of the responses they found most helpful was a private message of support.

One of the key questions I always ask when I start working with a survivor is, “What does justice look like to you?” We have grown up with the belief that rape must be reported. Going to the police isn’t everyone’s vision of justice, especially for marginalized communities that have harmful histories and current realities with the police. Plus, we know that there’s a prevalence of sexual violence committed by police themselves, with studies showing that sexual violence is the second most reported form of police misconduct. Responding by suggesting a survivor goes to the police may not help them feel supported. A better way to show support: ask them what they need. On my podcast, Healing Comes in Waves, I asked a survivor: “What did you do with your anger?” She told me no one had everasked her that. There is no right way to react to being sexually assaulted. Listening gives space for all the feelings.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How do you make sure they know you believe them? Validate their experience

The words that helped me breathe out shame from my body came from my friend, Kimiko, who quietly would tell me, “It’s not your fault,” “Your feelings make sense,” and “You’re not alone.”

Validating a survivor reminds them, and you, that the person responsible for sexual assault is the person who commits it. It doesn’t matter what the survivor drank, wore or texted the next day. The legal parameters around sexual assault are not my guide to understanding this harm. The understanding of this harm comes from my values.

Those words matter so much because survivors are hearing the opposite everywhere. Social media comments are flooded with, “Why was she drinking? Why did she go to his room? Why did she text him?” We heard a version of this recently on The View, when the conversation about Cornell turned to what she drank, what she took and what she’d agreed to earlier that night. Hear those interrogations long enough, and you start believing those excuses yourself. The reality is that consent is ongoing, and you can revoke it at any time. And if you are too intoxicated, you CANNOT give consent. Period. Blaming the survivor just puts the onus back on them as if they are the problem. It makes them question themselves. That’s exactly what happened to me after that conversation with my friend in the bathroom. And it’s not just me. A 2025 study of college women who had been assaulted found that when the people they told turned against them, they blamed themselves more, and that self-blame went hand in hand with more post-traumatic stress.

Shame and blame are what every survivor faces. Shame says, ” Don’t tell anyone.” Blame says, “It was your fault anyway.” I carried both.

Think about the last time someone said something awful to you. You were so stunned, you said nothing. Then, four days later, standing in the shower, you realize how awful it was. That’s what shock does. Now imagine it’s not words, but your body, and you’re afraid for your life. During a sexual assault, many survivors respond the way anyone would to the threat of being killed: we freeze, we go quiet, we do whatever we think will get us out alive. That’s survival. And still, afterward, we blame ourselves for it.

Having a drink, sending a text, wearing a tank top and shorts, or going to someone’s room does not constitute consent, and saying yes to one thing does not mean saying yes to everything that follows. Freezing isn’t consent either; it’s the body trying to survive.

Sexual assault can happen to all genders. We know that Trans and gender non-binary people are targeted for sexual violence at disproportionate rates due in part to the harmful, systemic narratives about them.

Men also face sexual assault. 7% of undergraduate men will be sexually assaulted. They are much more likely to be harmed than to be falsely accused. Stereotypes and assumptions of what it means is part of what silences men from ever talking about it.

Validation belongs to all survivors. Yet we know that Black, brown and Indigenous women — as well as other marginalized survivors — face discrimination within the legal system and in society at large. Days after the Cornell lawsuit, Kendall Francis, a Black first-generation student at LSU, spoke out. She says a football player assaulted her. LSU found him responsible for sexual assault and rape, then reduced his suspension to probation and let him back on the team. She went to the police herself, almost a year later, and says she failed both semesters of her first year. (He hasn’t been charged, and LSU says it followed its due process.) Her school believed her, and she was still left to carry it alone.

We’ve known for a long time that this falls hardest on Black girls and women. Too often, institutions and adults push the narrative onto Black girls that they are less innocent and less in need of protection than white girls, starting as young as five, Georgetown Law researchers found. And for Black women survivors, even milder negative reactions to disclosure have been linked to more PTSD and depression.

DashDividers_1_500x100

You don’t have to say the perfect thing. Just be there and empathize with their experience

Stay with them. Your presence matters more than perfect words. A simple text can do it: “Thank you for telling me. I know it must have been hard. I’m here for you.”

You don’t have to fix anything; staying is enough.

Give yourself grace. Bearing witness to someone’s harm has impacts, too, especially if you’re a survivor yourself. There are great resources like Chayn’s Bloom and MeToo Survivor Santaucy to access.

I think about that moment in the bathroom more than I think about him. What if my friend had seen me? In another world, maybe she would tell me. Maybe she was dealing with her own shame. She isn’t a monster; she is a product of a culture that would rather protect everyone’s peace than a woman’s right to safety.

“I believe you. It’s not your fault. What do you need?” When I think about that weekend years ago, it isn’t him that comes up. I think about my close friend in that bathroom, telling me not to ruin the trip. BRAVE is the conversation I deserved in that bathroom, and the one every survivor deserves.

So take it to the group chat. Check in with your people. You can simply say, “This story is heavy. It’s okay to take a break from the coverage. I’m going to leave the number for RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline: 800-656-HOPE. I know that many of us have gone through things like this, and we deserve care.” Your heart might pound when you hit send. It might feel awkward. Remember that awkward is what practice feels like in the body before it becomes culture. Being brave isn’t a one-time action; it’s continuously choosing to show up for each other.

There is always a survivor in the room, and that may include you. If that’s you, be gentle with yourself. To Jane Doe, survivor at the center of this story, and to the girl I was in that bathroom: I believe you.

If you’ve experienced sexual violence of any kind and need help or support, please visit Rainn or call 800-656-4673.

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
My father always pressured me to attend college, but he was very much in and out of my life growing up. My mom wanted my siblings and me to go to college, but she didn’t have much experience. I suspect she dropped out, but I’m not sure; she rarely talks about it. Either way, when it came time for me to complete my college applications, my father was nowhere to be found, and my mother was so overwhelmed by the process that she would have an emotional breakdown whenever I asked for help. That left me at 16 years old to navigate the entire process by myself. In hindsight, I wish I had gone to a state school, but I did a pre-college program at NYU and was determined to return to New York City for my undergraduate degree. I ended up graduating with $30,000 in student loan debt, which felt like a ridiculous amount of money at the time. 

After five years of work and setting myself up pretty well, I decided to return to school to become a psychologist. I had saved $20,000 in cash and thought that would get me through a two-year master’s program. Long story short, I ended up at one of the most expensive universities in the country and ended up with $200,000 of student loan debt and was ineligible to sit for licensure as a mental health professional. In hindsight, it wasn’t a smart decision, but honestly, I have no regrets, as it was the best two years of my life. 

So two years and $200,000 later, I still needed to obtain a license to practice psychology. In my first round of PhD/PsyD applications, I got two interviews and one acceptance. I didn’t want to try my luck again, so I’m at a NOT funded doctoral program, and here we are $419,000 in student loan debt and counting. I believe ~$85,000 is just accumulated interest. 

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
My father, an immigrant, was always ranting about how we need to save money but never actually taught us anything about saving or investing. My mother is the type of person to die with $100,000 in credit card debt as a “you gotcha” to credit companies. Growing up, I would see my mom with a huge stack of credit cards. Now that I know better, I worry about her retirement plan. My father isn’t in a great financial place either and basically says he’s broke any time I ask for anything.  

What was your first job and why did you get it?
I got my first job as a hostess at TGI Fridays at 16 to pay for gas for my car. I got a car as soon as I turned 16, mainly because my mom needed help driving my siblings to and from after-school activities. My money was mine, and I managed it independently, which was nice. At 16, I also accumulated a $3,000 debt to my university for my pre-college program, which I paid off in installments from age 17 to about 21.  

Did you worry about money growing up?
Yes, all the time. I was in charge of making “payment arrangements” for my mom for all the utilities in the house starting around the age of 13. Money was always tight growing up, and I didn’t play many recreational sports because of it. I also used my money from my hosting job to pay for my tennis and cheerleading camps. If I couldn’t afford it, I would rarely ask my mom to pay for it.  

Do you worry about money now?
Yes! I have been in denial about my student loan debt. I honestly thought I would practice abroad, but now that I’m in this relationship, I may be staying in the US after I graduate…which leads me to ask: how the hell am I going to pay off nearly half a million dollars? What would my monthly payment be? $5,000? My entire paycheck? It’s soul-crushing, but at this point I have to finish. I can’t have all of this debt and not even be a doctor at the end of it.

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I would honestly say as soon as I graduated college and perhaps even as early as high school. If I truly begged my parents for weeks on end, they would perhaps give me some financial support, but it’s not even worth the emotional energy at this point. As a psychologist in training, I have learned that I was a parentified child of two narcissists who don’t have the capacity to emotionally support me but will be elated to attend my graduation and brag to all of their friends that I’m a doctor due to their fantastic parenting.  

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
No, but I’ve been lucky enough to inherit intergenerational ~*`trauma`*~.

Beyond the luxurious, Old Hollywood-inspired packaging and iconic shades (case in point: Pillow Talk, the most famous nude shade in all of beauty), the formulas deliver the kind of long-wearing, high-performance results that have earned them a permanent spot in our beauty routines. (On top of that, the brand is a mainstay in any wedding day glam kit and a go-to of celebrity makeup artists, too.) Better yet, the brand rarely goes on sale, making this an extra special occurrence. 

Below, Refinery29’s beauty editors share the Charlotte Tilbury deals worth adding to your cart during the limited-time event. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lip Cheat Lip Liner in Pillow Talk, $28 $22.40

“No matter how many lip liners I try, I always come back to Charlotte Tilbury’s Lip Cheat. It’s the easiest to apply and one of the longest-lasting formulas I’ve used. In my experience, creamier lip liners tend to fade faster, so I like that this one has a slightly waxier texture, giving you more control during application while still being easy to blend. It grips to my lip line like Velcro and lasts well past lunchtime, often making it into the afternoon before I even think about topping it up. My go-to shade is Pillow Talk Medium, which has a browner undertone than the original Pillow Talk (the latter is a little too pink on me). I love how it subtly enhances my Cupid’s bow, making it look more defined and softly sculpted.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Beauty Director

Beauty Light Wand Glowgasm in Pinkgasm, $44 $35.20

There’s a reason it’s a go-to for brides! The sponge-tip applicator makes it incredibly easy to dab onto the cheeks, forehead, and nose for a seamless, sun-kissed look. Hollywood Blush & Glow (Rich Terracotta Blush/Golden Sunset Highlighter), $29 $20.30

While I’m not usually a highlighter person, this one delivers the prettiest candlelit glow that looks incredibly natural when applied with a light hand. I’ll even dust it across my eyelids as a shimmery eyeshadow to pull my whole look together. And at under $20 for Prime Day, it’s a no-brainer addition to this year’s haul.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer

Matte Beauty Blush Wand in Pillow Talk, $44 $35.20

“If shimmer isn’t your thing, consider Charlotte’s Matte Blush Wands. I attended a bride and bridesmaid makeup tutorial recently at the brand’s London flagship store, and these were the finishing touch in every look. They add life back into my skin after foundation, and I’m always surprised by how highly pigmented they are, despite being suspended in a creamy, moisturizing base. I rarely powder over it because the matte pigment really clings to the skin, but if you’re out and about or getting ready for a special occasion and want your makeup to last for hours on end, a light dusting of translucent powder will help lock it in. title: I Tried Gen Z’s Favorite New Way To Travel—And I Get The Hype
text:
I Tried Gen Z’s Favorite New Way To Travel—And I Get The Hype

I’m one of those people who wants to see the entire world. No flight is too long, no climate is off limits, and yes, I’m still manifesting a trip to Antarctica one day. There are really only two things standing between me and the ever-growing list of destinations in my Notes app: limited PTO and an unfortunately not-unlimited travel budget.

So when I heard about the way Gen Z is squeezing more travel into both, I was intrigued.

Airbnb calls it “lore-tripping”: skipping the obvious vacation destinations in favor of smaller, under-the-radar towns with interesting histories, local legend, and the kind of attractions you probably won’t find replicated in 15 other cities. And apparently, Gen Z is onto something. Airbnb surveyed a group of Gen Z travelers and found that 90% of them are interested in visiting small towns and under-the-radar destinations this fall, drawn by cheaper trips, local culture, and the thrill of finding somewhere that feels still undiscovered.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Best Places To Lore-Trip This Fall:

– Hot Springs, Arizona
– Helen, Georgia
– Point Pleasant, West Virginia
– Twentynine Palms, California
– Rapid City, South Dakota
– Williams, Arizona
– Wildwood, New Jersey
– Gibsonton, Florida
– Leavenworth, Washington
– Bemidji, Minnesota

DashDividers_1_500x100

Instead of automatically booking Paris, Miami, or another destination everyone on your Instagram feed has already visited, the idea is essentially to be the first in your group chat to discover somewhere new.

To chart my own new travel path, Airbnb invited me to spend a weekend lore-tripping in Twentynine Palms, California, a desert town just outside Joshua Tree National Park that is having a moment of its own. According to Airbnb, searches for Twentynine Palms among Gen Z travelers are up more than 50% this fall.

I went into the weekend thinking I was testing a here-today-gone-tomorrow travel trend, but I came back home wondering why I don’t take trips like this more often.

Getting Off The Grid — Literally

The beginning of the drive was familiar. Having made the trip from Los Angeles to Palm Springs for Coachella more times than I’d like to count, I recognized the seemingly endless rows of wind turbines almost immediately. But instead of stopping there, we kept going farther into the California desert, past mountains and those wonderfully strange sculptural Joshua trees until my husband and I reached our home for the weekend in Twentynine Palms.

We arrived at Casa Del Desierto⁠ just after sunset, which, admittedly, made my first introduction to lore-tripping slightly eerie. The house sits in the desert with few neighbors and very little artificial light around it. After living in cities for most of my adult life, I’m accustomed to streetlights, headlights, apartment windows, and the general glow of other human beings being nearby. Out here? Darkness. Desert. Silence.

By the next morning, the unfamiliar lull had become my favorite part.

I woke up before dawn and went outside to sit by the fire pit as the sun came up. The sky slowly turned this almost unbelievable orange-creamsicle shade that looked more like a painting than something happening directly in front of me. I meditated for a while and, for once, managed not to think about the frankly offensive number of unread emails waiting in my inbox. Of course I took pictures. I am still me. But eventually I put my phone down and just sat there.

That became an unexpected theme of the weekend. Lore-tripping made me want to disconnect in the best possible way and to just recharge with nature as the plug.

Now don’t get me wrong, the house definitely helped.

One of the advantages of choosing somewhere less obvious is that your accommodations can become part of the reason you take the trip rather than simply the place where you sleep between activities. Casa Del Desierto was spacious and peaceful, with the kind of indoor-outdoor setup that makes you actually want to stay put. There was a huge bathtub, his-and-hers showers, and the aforementioned fire pit, which quickly became our default spot whenever we had nowhere else to be.

And, because this is Refinery29, I should also mention: There were approximately a million places to take a good outfit photo.

My husband may have summed up the appeal better than I could. He described the desert’s energy as “infectious,” with an eccentric, earthy feeling unlike anywhere else. He loved how quiet it was, and told me he could see himself returning to Joshua Tree anytime he needed to clear his mind.

The stillness even followed him into his workouts. He went running outside, and without the usual soundtrack of traffic, sirens, and people rushing past him, exercise felt surprisingly meditative. My husband described running through the desert as making him feel closer to God: “It’s just me and nature,” he explained when he came back home.

I understood exactly what he meant.

The best part of the trip was finding places I wasn’t looking for. There’s a particular thrill to traveling somewhere famous. You finally see the monument, eat the thing, stand in the spot you’ve seen hundreds of times online. But there’s another kind of pleasure in arriving somewhere with almost no preconceived ideas about what you’re supposed to do.

That’s where lore-tripping really clicked for me.

A short drive from our Airbnb was Más o Menos, which may genuinely be one of the coolest coffee shops I’ve ever visited. I ordered a strawberry-banana matcha while a DJ played Lauryn Hill classics mixed with a ton of other feel-good sounds. And the coffee shop transforms into a 21-and-over hangout at night.

Then there was Kitchen in the Desert. This is one of those places that people should be driving from miles and miles away just to sit at chef Everton Gordon’s table. I have a habit when I travel: Once I find food I love, I will shamelessly go back rather than gambling on somewhere new. So yes, during a weekend-long trip, we ate there twice. The menu was fresh, unexpected, and exactly the kind of discovery that makes you immediately start recommending a place to friends.

None of it felt like we were working through a checklist of Things You Must Do In Twentynine Palms. We were just … there. Exploring. And maybe that’s the real luxury of going somewhere that isn’t overloaded with must-see landmarks.

So would I lore-trip again? Absolutely. I’m not suddenly giving up on Paris (or Antarctica, I’m still coming for you). But this trip changed the way I think about what actually qualifies as a vacation.

There’s a tendency to save our PTO and travel budgets for the big trips: the expensive flights, famous cities, packed itineraries, and destinations that require months of planning. Lore-tripping makes a convincing argument for the spaces in between. A weekend somewhere unexpected can still give you the feeling I’m usually chasing halfway around the world: discovery.

And apparently, I’m not alone. Airbnb says 60% of surveyed travelers are planning a weekend getaway this fall, and its data shows that more weekend trips happened during fall than any other season in 2025.
For travelers trying to see more of the world without unlimited money or vacation days, perhaps the answer isn’t always figuring out how to go farther. That random town you always drive past might be the getaway you never knew you needed.

title: Blakely Thornton on Pop Culture, Gay Beauty Standards, and What Makes An It Girl
text:
Blakely Thornton on Pop Culture, Gay Beauty Standards, and What Makes An It Girl

Blakely Thornton is an original. A self-described Pop Culture Anthropologist and Out 100 Honoree, Blakely has built a digital career that uniquely spans comedy, entertainment, and style. On social media, fans flock to him for his honest, no-holds-barred commentary on their favorite topics. Others tune into Yestergays to hear him and his podcast co-host critique fashion and celebrity culture with his signature wit. Celebrities are smitten with him, often tickled by their engagements at red carpet events like the Met Gala and ultra-exclusive gyms. This very public, creative life wasn’t what Blakely imagined for himself as an athletic kid growing up in Dallas, Texas. Blakely was a closeted football player at UPenn, majoring in finance and hoping to follow in his parents’ footsteps into a respectable, stable career. Headed towards a traditionally corporate career, Blakely worked at Ralph Lauren and pursued the corporate finance life until he didn’t.

Eventually, Blakely decided that he wouldn’t spend another twenty years as anything other than his full self, and it has paid off. Instead of trying to find ways to inject creativity into a 9-5, Blakely leverages his taste and honesty into a living. During our conversation, we cover everything pop culture, from GLP1s to what makes an It Girl to how much attention Zendaya is actually generating for films and fashion houses. We cover the other side of being very popular online, like the mean comments on Reddit, being seen only as a product, and being expected to carry the emotional weight of a fanbase. Blakely is open about the mental and emotional safeguards he needs to manage the opinions of hundreds of thousands of fans, and why he turns to working out to maintain his peace of mind. We also chat about misogynistic beauty standards, how he makes friends with so many celebrities, and why Heated Rivalry was so impactful.

title: Trichologist Ashley Zsaton: Hair Restoration, Growth Supplements & Protective Styles
text:
Trichologist Ashley Zsaton: Hair Restoration, Growth Supplements & Protective Styles

Ashley Zsaton, DNP, ACNP-AG, learned about hair politics early. Growing up biracial in Milwaukee, she wasn’t always accepted for wearing her natural curls. Her search to understand what people meant by “good” and “bad” hair led her to become a board-certified nurse practitioner and hair loss specialist. As co-founder of the Hollywood Hair Institute, California’s preeminent hair transplant & aesthetic treatment center, Dr. Zsaton established herself as a leading hair restoration specialist and trichologist. Her medical background also includes supporting patients in critical conditions in the ICU and in ophthalmology, where her research led to the national publication of a school-based vision screening program. But before she began her medical career, she was trying to develop a healthy relationship with her own hair. A move to the Dominican Republic opened her eyes to the incredible beauty and versatility of naturally curly hair.

In the Dominican Republic, Dr. Zsaton was exposed to a country filled with curly hair styled and cared for in all manner of styles. She brought this newfound passion for hair back to the States, and when she decided to pursue a career in medicine, her husband encouraged her to follow her interest in scalp care towards medical aesthetics. Fast forward to now, and Dr. Zsaton is changing lives by helping people access the hair restoration treatments that are best for them. During our conversation, we discussed every hair restoration treatment from PRP to Follicular Unit Extraction to Minoxidil. Dr. Zsaton walked host, Brooke Devard, through what a good surgical candidate profile looks like, and which alternatives may be a better fit for her patients. In fact, Brooke walked through the exact routine Dr. Zsaton prepared for her and detailed how effective each product has been in growing her hair. Dr. Zsaton doesn’t hold back when it comes to sharing which hairstyles may be causing the most damage, traction alopecia, for both men and women, and which products aren’t doing anything helpful at all. She gives a peek into the aesthetic innovations she’s explored in Turkey and Korea that she’d like to offer her patients here in the States. Dr. Zsaton offered an unfiltered, honest look at the limits and possibilities of hair restoration.
